title: Hazardous Areas - North America Classification
description: A comprehensive tool for understanding and classifying hazardous areas in North America using both the Class/Division/Group system and the Zone/Group system. Determine required protection techniques for electrical installations in locations with flammable gases, vapors, combustible dusts, or ignitable fibers.

components.content:
## Hazardous Areas - North America Classification

Electrical equipment installation in atmosphere with flammable gases or vapors, flammable liquids, combustible dusts, ignitable fibers or flyings represents a risk for fire and explosion.

Areas with possible fire or explosion risks due to explosive atmospheres are classified using the **Class/Division** system (North America) or the **Zone** system (Europe and increasingly North America).

### Classification Systems

#### Class/Division/Group System
Based on Article 500 of the National Electrical Code (NEC):
- **Classes** - General nature of the hazardous material
- **Divisions** - Probability of hazardous material being present
- **Groups** - Type of the hazardous material

#### Zone/Group System
Based on Articles 505/506 of the National Electrical Code (NEC):
- **Zones** - General nature and probability of hazardous material
- **Groups** - Type of hazardous material and location

components.content:
## Class/Division/Group System Details

### Classes
- **Class I**: Flammable gases or vapors
- **Class II**: Combustible or conductive dusts
- **Class III**: Ignitable fibers or flyings

### Divisions
- **Division 1**: High probability - continuous, intermittent, or periodic presence under normal operating conditions
- **Division 2**: Low probability - abnormal conditions only, short duration

### Groups (Class I: A-D for Gases)
- **Group A**: Acetylene
- **Group B**: MESG ≤ 0.45mm or MIC ≤ 0.40 (Hydrogen, Fuel gases with >30% hydrogen)
- **Group C**: MESG > 0.75mm or 0.40 < MIC < 0.80 (Carbon monoxide, Ether, Hydrogen sulfide)
- **Group D**: MESG > 0.75mm or MIC > 0.80 (Gasoline, Acetone, Ammonia, Benzene, Propane)

### Groups (Class II & III: E-G for Dusts)
- **Group E**: Combustible metal dusts (Aluminum, Magnesium, Titanium, Zinc)
- **Group F**: Carbonaceous dusts (Coal, Carbon black, with >8% volatiles)
- **Group G**: Other combustible dusts (Flour, Grain, Starch, Sugar, Wood, Plastics)

## Zone/Group System Details

### Zones - Gases, Vapors, Mists
- **Zone 0**: Present continuously or for long periods
- **Zone 1**: Likely to occur under normal operating conditions
- **Zone 2**: Not likely under normal conditions, short period only

### Zones - Dusts
- **Zone 20**: Dusts present continuously or for long periods
- **Zone 21**: Dusts likely to occur under normal operating conditions
- **Zone 22**: Dusts not likely under normal conditions, short period only

### Groups
- **Group I**: Mining locations with firedamp
- **Group II**: Explosive gas atmospheres (Zones 0, 1, 2)
  - **IIA**: Propane, Acetone, Benzene, Butane, Methane, Petrol
  - **IIB**: Ethylene, Propylene oxide, Ethylene oxide, Butadiene
  - **IIC**: Acetylene, Hydrogen, Carbon disulphide
- **Group III**: Explosive dust atmospheres (Zones 20, 21, 22)
  - **IIIA**: Combustible flyings
  - **IIIB**: Non-conductive dust
  - **IIIC**: Conductive dust

## Example
A propane gas installation would typically be classified as:
- **Class/Division**: Class I, Division 2, Group D
- **Zone System**: Zone 2, Group IIA
